question.worked_solution:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-{630}^{∘}$ that lies in the range $[0,{360}^{∘}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{630}^{∘}+{360}^{∘} & =-{270}^{∘} \\ -{630}^{∘}+2\cdot {360}^{∘} & ={90}^{∘}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(-{630}^{∘})=\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘}).$

The angle ${90}^{∘}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266176/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${90}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡({90}^{∘})=1.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(-{630}^{∘})=1.$
